label: Supply-chain due diligence and transparency laws
source: National legislation databases (legislation.gov.uk, Assemblée nationale / Légifrance, legislation.gov.au, gesetze-im-internet.de, Fedlex, Justice Laws Canada), Norwegian Consumer Authority, EUR-Lex
method: States with a binding national statute in force that requires companies to report on (transparency) or act on (due diligence) forced labour, child labour or human rights in their supply chains; v is the stronger obligation in force. EU laws are kept in a separate note (eu_note) because neither applies yet: the CSDDD from 26 Jul 2029 and the Forced Labour Regulation from 14 Dec 2027. Not counted: the Netherlands Child Labour Due Diligence Act (Wet zorgplicht kinderarbeid, Stb. 2019, 401), adopted but only to start on a date set by royal decree, with no commencement found; sub-national laws such as the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act (2012) and the New South Wales Modern Slavery Act 2018; US federal import bans (Tariff Act s.307, Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act), which bar goods rather than require company reporting or due diligence; bills not yet passed (e.g. South Korea); and EU sector rules such as the Conflict Minerals Regulation (EU) 2017/821.

GBR.text: Modern Slavery Act 2015, s.54 (in force 29 Oct 2015): commercial organisations supplying goods or services with turnover of £36m or more must publish an annual slavery and human trafficking statement.

FRA.text: Loi n° 2017-399 relative au devoir de vigilance (27 Mar 2017): companies with 5,000+ employees in France or 10,000+ worldwide (with subsidiaries) must draw up and carry out a vigilance plan covering human rights and the environment.

AUS.text: Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) (in force 1 Jan 2019): entities based or operating in Australia with consolidated revenue over A$100m must report annually on modern slavery risks in operations and supply chains.

DEU.text: Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz (LkSG) (in force 1 Jan 2023): companies with 3,000+ employees in Germany, 1,000+ from 1 Jan 2024, must carry out human rights and environmental due diligence in their supply chains. An amending bill to cut reporting was before the Bundestag in 2026.

NOR.text: Transparency Act (Åpenhetsloven) (in force 1 Jul 2022): larger enterprises (2 of 3: NOK 70m sales, NOK 35m balance sheet, 50 FTE) must carry out human rights due diligence, publish an account and answer information requests.

CHE.text: Code of Obligations arts. 964j-964l and Ordinance DDTrO (in force 1 Jan 2022): companies importing or processing conflict minerals above set amounts, or with reasonable grounds to suspect child labour, must exercise due diligence and report; SMEs (below 2 of 3: CHF 20m assets, CHF 40m revenue, 250 FTE) and low-risk firms are exempt.

CAN.text: Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act, S.C. 2023, c. 9 (Bill S-211; in force 1 Jan 2024): government institutions and entities listed in Canada, or meeting 2 of 3 (C$20m assets, C$40m revenue, 250 employees), must report annually on forced and child labour risks.

eu_note.text: EU-wide laws, not yet applying: the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU) 2024/1760, as amended by Directive (EU) 2026/470 (Omnibus I), must be transposed by 26 Jul 2028 and applies from 26 Jul 2029 to companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn worldwide turnover (non-EU companies: EUR 1.5bn EU turnover). The Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 (in force 13 Dec 2024) bans products made with forced labour from the EU market from 14 Dec 2027.

laws.name: Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU) 2024/1760
laws.scope: more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover; non-EU companies with EUR 1.5bn EU turnover

laws.name: Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015
laws.scope: all economic operators placing or making available products on the EU market or exporting them, any size
